paper_a.title: Distribution of Eigenvalues for Some Sets of Random Matrices (Marchenko & Pastur, 1967)

paper_b.title: Characteristic Vectors of Bordered Matrices With Infinite Dimensions (Wigner, 1955)

metadata.description: Marchenko-Pastur (paper A, 1967) extends Wigner's semicircle setting (paper B, 1955) to a much broader ensemble: a deterministic self-adjoint operator $A_N$ perturbed by an arbitrary number of i.i.d. rank-one operators $\tau_i (\cdot, q^{(i)}) q^{(i)}$, governed by a concentration $c = \lim n/N$ and a coefficient distribution $\sigma(\tau)$. Where Wigner derives the semicircle density via the combinatorial moment method (Catalan path counts), MP derives a fixed-point integral / Stieltjes-transform equation whose solution is unique. The classical semicircle reappears as the $c \to \infty$ limit of MP's canonical example (ExP321.1, RP321.1), and MP explicitly cites Wigner's 1958 semicircle as TP321.4. Both papers are PDF-fallback extractions, so we lean on `name`/`type` over exact LaTeX. The relationship is best described as EXT (MP generalizes the semicircle setup); SM (same method) does NOT fit because the two derivations use different machinery (Stieltjes transform fixed point vs. moment method).

matches.explanation: MP's $B_N(n) = A_N + \sum_i \tau_i (\cdot, q^{(i)}) q^{(i)}$ (DP321.1) is the strict generalization of Wigner's two random matrix definitions: the bordered matrix $H = \mathbf{k} + \mathbf{v}$ (DP322.1, with $A_N$ playing the role of the integer diagonal $\mathbf{k}$) and the random-sign symmetric matrix $H_0$ (DP322.2, the case $A_N = 0$ with rank-one structure encoded by random signs). MP's perturbations are rank-one with continuous coefficient distribution $\sigma$; Wigner's are dense with discrete $\pm v$ entries. Same conceptual role (the random Hermitian operator under study), different formulation.

MP's normalized spectral function $\nu(\lambda; B_N)$ (DP321.2) is the empirical CDF of eigenvalues. Wigner's strength function $S(x)$ / its derivative $\sigma(x)$ (DP322.3) is the cumulative mass of squared 0-components of eigenvectors weighted by eigenvalues; in his random-sign symmetric ensemble the strength function and the eigenvalue density coincide (cf. PrP322.1, TP322.3 conclusion). Different objects in general but playing the analogous role of 'the limiting spectral object we want to characterize'.

MP's concentration parameter $c = \lim n/N$ (DP321.3) controls the ratio of perturbations to ambient dimension. Wigner's setup has no analogue: there is no separately tuned 'number of perturbations' relative to dimension; his border has size $2N+1$ and is automatically dense. The closest analogue is $q = v^2/N$ in the wide-border ensemble, but $q$ is a coupling strength, not a concentration.

MP's Stieltjes transform $m(z; c) = \int (\lambda - z)^{-1} d\nu$ with its inversion formula (DP321.4) is the central analytic tool of the paper. Wigner does not use the Stieltjes transform at all: he works directly with the moments of $S(x)$ and inverts via Bessel-function Fourier transform (PSP322.5). This is precisely the methodological gap that makes the relation EXT rather than SM.

MP's generalized inverse $\tau(\xi)$ of the coefficient distribution $\sigma(x)$ (DP321.5) and its empirical version $\sigma(x, T_n)$ / $\tau(\xi, T_n)$ (DP321.6) are bookkeeping for the i.i.d. coefficients $\tau_i$. Wigner has no random coefficients in his ensembles (only $\pm v$ signs and a fixed magnitude), so these have no counterpart.

MP's Conditions I-IV (concentration limit, convergence of $\nu(\lambda; A_N)$, fourth-moment factorisation for $q^{(i)}$, i.i.d. $\tau_i$) are explicit assumptions enabling the general theorem. Wigner's setup is concrete (specific ensembles) and does not isolate analogous standing hypotheses, beyond passing comments about the ensemble distributions.

MP's main theorem (TP321.1) is the strict generalization of Wigner's two limiting-density theorems. TP322.3 (semicircle for random-sign symmetric) is recovered from MP by specialising to $A_N = 0$, $\tau_i$ a constant, and taking $c \to \infty$ (this limiting case is recorded explicitly in MP as ExP321.1 and RP321.1). TP322.6 (the wide-border integral equation $\rho = q R_1 \int \ldots$) is itself a generalisation of TP322.3 in Wigner's own paper, also subsumed by MP. MP states the result for arbitrary self-adjoint $A_N$ and arbitrary coefficient law $\sigma$, with the limit characterised by the unique solution of a fixed-point integral equation; Wigner's statements are special cases with explicit closed-form densities.

MP's Theorem 2 (TP321.2: continuous-deformation generalization with $\tau(t)$ continuous on $[0,1]$ and Stieltjes transform given implicitly via $w = z \exp(c \int \ldots)$) and Wigner's wide-border integral equation TP322.6 both characterize the limiting spectral object via an implicit/integral equation in the regime where $v$ (or $\tau$) varies along the matrix. Both yield existence-uniqueness of the limit measure rather than a closed-form density. MP's framework is more general; Wigner gives the wide-border formula in the specific scaling $v^2/N = q$ fixed.
MP's Theorem 3 (random unitary matrices via products of phase-rotation rank-one perturbations) has no Wigner counterpart; Wigner restricts attention to Hermitian / real symmetric ensembles.

MP cites Wigner's 1958 semicircle law as TP321.4 (origin: external, citing 'Wigner, Ann. of Math. 67 (1958), 325-327'). Paper B's TP322.3 is Wigner's earlier 1955 derivation of the same semicircle density $(8Nv^2 - x^2)^{1/2}/(4\pi N v^2)$ for the random-sign symmetric ensemble. This is the canonical paper-origin (Wigner 1955) ↔ external-citation (in MP) match: MP cites the 1958 follow-up while paper B is the 1955 original; the underlying mathematical content (semicircle density for a Wigner-type ensemble) is identical. This match is signal for relation_type EXT.

MP cites Glivenko's theorem (TP321.5, external) for almost-sure uniform convergence of empirical distributions to handle the random $\tau_i$. Wigner has no random coefficient distribution and no use for Glivenko.

MP's master equation $m(z;c) = -[z - c\int \tau d\sigma/(1+\tau m)]^{-1}$ (EP321.1), its PDE form (EP321.2), and the spectrum-edge relation $x(m;c)$ (EP321.3) constitute the closed analytic system characterizing the limiting Stieltjes transform. Wigner's wide-border moment recursion (EP322.7) and integral equation $\rho(\zeta) = qR_1(\zeta)\int (\rho(z)-\rho(\zeta))/(\zeta^2-z^2)dz + qR_1\rho \int \ldots$ (EP322.8) play the analogous role for his wide-border ensemble: a fixed-point/integral characterization of the limiting density. The objects differ (Stieltjes transform vs. density itself; smooth coefficient law vs. fixed magnitude $q$), but both are 'the equation that pins down the limit'.

MP's algorithmic 'spectrum-boundary determination rule' (AP321.1: form $x(m;c)$, find monotonicity intervals, read off edges and singularity exponents) is an analytical procedure attached to the Stieltjes transform machinery. Wigner has no analogous procedure; his density is given directly in closed form (semicircle) or implicitly via moments / integral equation, and he does not extract edge singularities by algorithm.

MP's Lemma 1 (LP321.1: quadratic-form concentration $|(Aq,q) - N^{-1}\mathrm{Sp}\,A| \le \|A\|\varepsilon(N)$) is a probabilistic concentration bound for random vectors $q$ satisfying the fourth-moment condition III. Wigner's combinatorial moment method computes $\mathrm{Av}(H^{2\nu})_{00}$ directly by averaging over signs (PSP322.2) and never invokes a generic quadratic-form concentration lemma; the role of randomness control is played by the parity-of-edge-traversal selection rule.

MP's Lemma 2 (LP321.2: trace-difference identity $\mathrm{Sp}\,\tilde R_z - \mathrm{Sp}\,R_z = -d/dz\,\ln[1 + \tau(R_z q,q)] + \delta$ for rank-one perturbations) is the analytic engine of the Stieltjes-transform approach. No counterpart in Wigner's moment-method derivation.
MP's Lemma 3 (LP321.3: $L^1$ convergence of empirical inverse $\tau(\xi, T_n) \to \tau(\xi)$) handles the random coefficient distribution. Wigner has no random coefficient law.

MP's Lemma 4 (LP321.4: convergence of $u(z, \xi; N, T_n, Q_n)$ to the integral equation, in mean) is the 'existence' half of the main result. Wigner's analogue would be 'the moments converge to Catalan numbers', but that is built into his counting argument and not isolated as a separate convergence lemma in the same form.

Both papers need a uniqueness statement to identify the limit. MP's Lemma 5 (LP321.5) proves uniqueness of solutions to the integral equation $u(z,t) = m_0(z) - c\int \ldots$ within a class of holomorphic functions, via a Haar-style maximum-modulus contradiction. Wigner invokes the Carleman/Perron-Carleman moment-uniqueness theorem (TP322.5, cited from Carleman 1926) to assert that the moments $\{T_\nu\}$ uniquely determine the wide-border density. Same conceptual role (uniqueness of the limiting spectral measure), achieved via different machinery (PDE-uniqueness vs. moment problem).

PP321.6 is MP's proof of Theorem 1 (combine Lemma 4 existence + Lemma 5 uniqueness, then truncate to lift bounded $\tau$ to general). PP322.3 is Wigner's proof of the semicircle (TP322.3) via the moment method (compute even moments, count valid sequences, solve Catalan recursion, invert via Bessel Fourier transform). PP322.4 proves the wide-border integral equation TP322.6 by a path decomposition giving the bilinear moment recursion plus Carleman uniqueness. Same end goal (limiting spectral law) via fundamentally different proof strategies; this is the central methodological contrast that drives the EXT classification (and the reason SM does NOT fit). The proof-step DAGs differ enough that no composite L2 entry adds value beyond this parent-level alignment.

MP's auxiliary proofs (PP321.1 Lemma 1 quadratic-form concentration; PP321.2 Lemma 2 trace-difference identity via determinant lemma; PP321.3 Lemma 3 via Glivenko + truncation; PP321.4 Lemma 4 chaining rank-one perturbations into the integral equation; PP321.5 Lemma 5 Haar-contradiction uniqueness) are tied to the Stieltjes-transform machinery and the random coefficient law. They have no counterparts among Wigner's proofs (PP322.1 sign-conjugation symmetry, PP322.2 Bessel-recurrence, PP322.3 moment method, PP322.4 path decomposition for wide border).

Wigner's definition of moments $M_\nu = \int x^\nu dS(x)$ (DP322.4) anchors his entire moment-method derivation. MP does not use moments at all (it works with the Stieltjes transform $m(z;c)$), so this central object of paper B has no counterpart in paper A.

Wigner's combinatorial machinery — valid (closed-walk, even-edge-multiplicity) sequences DP322.5 and their type-sequence encoding DP322.6 (Catalan-counted) — is specific to the moment method. MP has no path-counting / combinatorial encoding.

Wigner's eigenvalue equation $H\psi = \lambda\psi$ (EP322.1) is the trivial spectral relation. MP also studies eigenvalues but never writes the eigenvalue equation explicitly as a separate node; it works at the level of the spectral measure $\nu$ and its Stieltjes transform. Treated as 'no explicit counterpart' on the MP side, low confidence because one could argue MP implicitly uses the same equation.

Wigner's singly bordered ($N=1$) recurrence $-v\psi_{l-1} + l\psi_l - v\psi_{l+1} = 0$ (EP322.2) and Bessel-form solution $\psi_l = J_l(2v)$ (EP322.3) belong to the integer-spectrum / Bessel-eigenvector subsection (TP322.1, TP322.2), which is unique to paper B and has no MP counterpart.

Wigner's Catalan moment formula (EP322.4), the type-sequence generating function $t(x) = 1 + xt(x)^2$ (EP322.5), and the explicit semicircle density (EP322.6) are downstream of the moment method. MP also yields the semicircle density in ExP321.1 / RP321.1 as a limiting case, but via the Stieltjes-transform fixed point, not via these closed-form combinatorial expressions; MP has no equation-level counterpart for these specific combinatorial identities.

Wigner's small-$q$ Lorentzian and large-$\zeta$ super-exponential asymptotics (EP322.9, EP322.10) for the wide-border strength function are paper-B-specific asymptotic analyses with no MP counterpart.
Wigner's singly bordered ($N=1$) eigenproblem (ProbP322.1) is a special low-dimensional spectral problem with explicit Bessel-function solution. MP does not consider singly bordered matrices.

Wigner's two limiting-spectrum problems (ProbP322.2: random-sign symmetric strength function; ProbP322.3: wide-border strength function) are subsumed by MP's single problem 'find the limiting normalized spectral function $\nu(\lambda; c)$ of $B_N(n)$'. MP doesn't isolate this as a `problem` node, but its Theorem 1 (TP321.1) is exactly the answer; the natural alignment is Wigner's two problems ↔ MP's general theorem statement (already covered by the TP321.1 ↔ TP322.3+TP322.6 match above). Listed as analogous-with-no-A-counterpart at the problem-node level for completeness.

Wigner's results that the singly bordered eigenvalues are the integers (TP322.1) and that the eigenvectors are Bessel functions $J_{l-k}(2v)$ (TP322.2) belong to the singly bordered ($N=1$) sub-investigation, which is paper-B-specific and disjoint from MP's content.
